video.title: Fix Your Forehand Over-Rotation | 3 Counter-Rotational Balance Techniques

classification.reason: The coach explains the biomechanics of counter-rotational braking on the forehand, demonstrates three variations, and details practice methods.

problem.title_as_question: How can you fix forehand over-rotation using counter-rotational balance techniques?
problem.definition: Players often continuously twist their hips through contact rather than using transient rotation and counter-rotational braking, leading to slower, less accurate shots and spinning out past the target.
prerequisites: Hitting from open or semi-open stances

symptoms.description: The player hits forehands both slower and less accurately due to failing to control rotation through the hitting zone.
The player's body and torso spin out past the shot instead of staying on a linear path through the hitting zone.
The front foot heel lifts off the ground and twists out before or at contact, causing the shot to miss wide.

causes.statement: The player's hip rotation twists continuously all the way through contact rather than being transient and stopping.
The player lacks a counter-rotational movement from the lower body in the opposite direction to slow or stop hip rotation through the hitting zone.
The player allows the front foot to twist out and lift rather than pressing static force into the ground to resist continuing rotation.

angles.summary: Forehand hip rotation must be transient (starts and stops) so that arresting the hips creates a whip effect that lets the torso flick through.
Roger Federer demonstrates both the right leg kicking back and the left leg lifting forward to execute counter-rotational braking on inside-out forehands.
MLB pitchers like Jacob deGrom brace against their front leg at release to arrest rotational force and transfer it into linear momentum.
The coach contrasts letting the front foot lift and twist out (causing a miss wide) against keeping the front foot planted to resist over-rotation.
Players often mistakenly believe the front-foot hop happens at contact, whereas pros remain firmly planted through contact and only hop on the follow-through.

solutions.summary: Practice driving through the hitting hip such that the hitting leg kicks back behind the body while sending the entire body forward on a line.
Practice early swing driving motions using a medicine ball to build force production and counter-rotational sequencing through heightened kinesthetic feedback.
Pause video right at contact to check whether the front foot remains firmly planted and pressing into the ground rather than having the heel lift off early.
